newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr rallies, breaks 90 yen barrier.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr rallies, breaks 90 yen barrier.

text.p: The Australian dollar found relief from nagging interest rate concerns Monday as a worldwide migration to high yielding currencies boosted it on the crosses.
Growing speculation of a imminent cut in rates had seen support beneath 79 cents threatened this morning, but the Reserve Bank held silent and gave it another day of grace.

Relief turned to outright bullishness as waves of Japanese buying, some of it linked to samurai bond issues, swamped a short market and propelled the dollar decisively through the 90.00 yen barrier for the first time in more than four years.
By 4.45 pm (0530 GMT) the local currency had crested at 90.30/40 yen after surging from an opening 89.59/69 and Friday's late 89.73/83.
That was the highest close since September 1994 and brought the dollar's gains so far this year to 13 yen or 17 percent.
"The Aussie just cruised through the 90.00 yen level," said Andrew McGill, a forex sales dealer at Chase. "It was an impressive performance and bodes well for more gains ahead."
Dealers said the initial impetus came from a single A$330 million buy order linked to a yen/A$ dual currency samurai bond for the Canadian province of Ontario.
Straight demand followed from Tokyo and U.S. funds were also seen playing the carry trade -- borrowing in yen where rates are at record lows and lending in dollars for much higher returns.

In contrast the local currency was subdued on the U.S. dollar, where it has much less of a yield advantage. It did edge up to US$0.7925/30 from an early US$0.7903/08 but was still short of Friday's late US$0.7938/43.
That held it steady on its trade weighted index at 58.7.
Analysts said the yen's weakness reflected the growing market conviction Japanese rates would remain at their record lows for the foreseeable future.
That belief saw Japanese 10-yr bond yields ease to a year low of 2.610 percent today, a long way below the comparable Australian yield of 7.39 percent.

A cut in domestic short term rates -- which looked likely some time in the next month -- could dim the dollar's lustre, although dealers noted that bond yields here had already priced in a 0.5 point cut in official rates to 6.5 percent.
Any cut was also likely be seen as the last in the easing cycle which should further limiting the damage.
The market's preoccupation with monetary policy will colour the reaction to all this week's domestic, and offshore, data.
The September current account on Wednesday is expected to show the deficit remained at a tolerable A$1.3 billion from A$1.33 billion in August.
Such a result would also promise a big boost to Q3 GDP growth from next exports in the order of 0.6 to 1.0 percent.
That would support dollar sentiment at the margin but would have little implication for monetary policy, analysts said.

In this regard, building approvals on Thursday and retail sales Friday have more potential to influence market thoughts on policy. Approvals are forecast to be flat as a pay-back for solid gains of 1.6 percent in August and 8.1 percent in July.
A similar payback is also expected for retail sales which are seen dipping 0.5 percent in September after healthy gains of 1.1 and 1.0 percent in August and July respectively.
Such a dip would still mean real sales for the third quarter rose a hefty 1.3 percent and consumer spending again made a solid contribution to GDP growth for the quarter.

The probability of a domestic cut had been well priced into the local dollar, but the risk of a U.S. rate rise may return to haunt it depending on a welter of U.S. economic data this week. These include key reports on wages, GDP, employment and business sentiment. -- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
